courses.title: The Indian monsoon
courses.summary: See how land-sea heating, the Himalayas and the Western Ghats drive India's monsoon rains.
outcomes: Explain how land-sea temperature difference creates monsoon winds
Describe the two branches of the south-west monsoon

steps.title: Land and sea
steps.body: Land heats faster than sea in summer, forming a low over land and high over sea. Air flows from high to low pressure, carrying moisture inland.

steps.title: Importance
steps.body: About 70% of India's annual rainfall comes in the south-west monsoon months (June-September), and agriculture depends on it.

objects.label: Indian peninsula
objects.info: The land that heats quickly in summer. Heated air rises and creates low pressure over north-west India.

objects.label: Arabian Sea
objects.info: Source of moist south-west winds for the west coast. Seas heat more slowly than land.

objects.label: Bay of Bengal
objects.info: The second branch of the monsoon draws moisture from here for eastern and northern India.

objects.label: Himalayas
objects.info: A great barrier that stops the monsoon clouds moving north, forcing rain over the plains, and blocks cold air from Central Asia.

objects.label: Western Ghats
objects.info: Moist winds are forced up the western slopes, cool and drop heavy orographic rain; the eastern side lies in a rain shadow.

objects.label: Thermal low (north-west India)
objects.info: In May-June the Thar region and north-west plains get intensely hot. Rising air creates low pressure that pulls in moist air from the sea.

objects.label: South-west monsoon (Arabian Sea branch)
objects.info: Moist winds bring rain to Kerala around 1 June on average, then move up the west coast.

objects.label: South-west monsoon (Bay branch)
objects.info: Turns west along the Himalayas, bringing rain to eastern and northern India.

objects.label: ITCZ shifts north
objects.info: The Intertropical Convergence Zone, a belt of rising air near the equator, shifts north in summer, helping the monsoon onset.

objects.label: Kerala onset

objects.label: North-east monsoon (winter)

courses.title: Inside a volcano
courses.summary: Slice a volcano in 3D: magma chamber, conduit, vent, crater, lava, ash and layered cone.
outcomes: Name the parts of a volcano
Explain why volcanoes erupt
Contrast shield and stratovolcanoes
Describe hazards and safety

scenes.text: Shake a soda bottle and open it.

steps.title: Magma path
steps.body: Magma collects in a chamber, rises through the conduit and erupts at the vent as lava, gas and ash.

steps.title: India
steps.body: Barren Island in the Andaman Sea is India's only confirmed active volcano. The ancient Deccan Traps are a huge lava plateau formed about 66 million years ago.

activity.prompt: Explode the volcano and follow the magma path.

objects.label: Crust and mantle rock
objects.info: Solid rock above the magma. Magma rises because it is less dense than the rock around it.

objects.label: Magma chamber
objects.info: A large reservoir of molten rock a few to tens of kilometres underground. Gas dissolved in the magma drives eruptions.

objects.label: Conduit (main pipe)
objects.info: The channel magma travels up to reach the surface.

objects.label: Volcanic cone
objects.info: Built from layers of lava and ash from past eruptions, so it grows upward over time.

objects.label: Crater and vent
objects.info: The bowl at the summit where magma and gas erupt.

objects.label: Lava flow
objects.info: Magma that reaches the surface is called lava. Basalt lava is runny and can flow for kilometres; sticky lavas pile up near the vent.

objects.label: Ash cloud
objects.info: Fine fragments of rock and glass thrown into the air. Ash can travel hundreds of kilometres, closing airports and harming lungs.

objects.label: Volcanic bombs
objects.info: Blobs of molten rock thrown out during eruption that cool in the air.

objects.label: Dike and side vent
objects.info: Magma can also squeeze through cracks (dikes) and erupt from a side vent.

objects.label: Alternating layers
objects.info: Layers of ash and lava make a stratovolcano. They give the cone its steep, layered structure.

objects.label: Plate boundary
objects.info: Many volcanoes lie where plates collide (subduction) or spread apart, such as the Ring of Fire around the Pacific. Hotspots like Hawaii are another cause.

objects.label: Gas bubbles
objects.info: Dissolved gases (water vapour, CO2, SO2) expand as magma rises, like opening a fizzy drink, driving explosive eruptions.

quiz.q: What is molten rock underground called?
quiz.why: It is called lava once it erupts.

steps.title: Types
steps.body: Shield volcanoes have gentle slopes from runny basalt lava (e.g. Mauna Loa). Stratovolcanoes are steep, layered cones from alternating lava and ash (e.g. Mount Fuji).

steps.title: Largest

steps.title: Surface currents
steps.body: Prevailing winds push surface water. The Coriolis effect (from Earth's rotation) bends flow right in the northern hemisphere and left in the south, producing circular gyres.

steps.title: Speed
steps.body: The Gulf Stream moves at up to about 2 m/s and carries about 30 times the flow of all the world's rivers combined.

steps.title: Doubling rule

objects.label: Sun
objects.info: Our star: a ball of hydrogen and helium about 1.39 million km across. It holds 99.86% of the solar system's mass and fusion in its core makes its light.

objects.label: Mercury
objects.info: Smallest planet and closest to the Sun. It circles the Sun in 88 days, has almost no air, and swings from very hot days to freezing nights.

objects.label: Venus
objects.info: Wrapped in thick carbon-dioxide clouds, with a surface near 465 °C - hotter than Mercury. It spins backwards compared with most planets.

objects.label: Earth
objects.info: The only world known to have life and liquid oceans on its surface. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach it.

objects.label: Mars
objects.info: The red planet, coloured by iron oxide dust. It has Olympus Mons, the tallest known volcano in the solar system (about 22 km high), and two tiny moons.

objects.label: Asteroid belt
objects.info: A region of rocky leftovers between Mars and Jupiter. Despite films, the asteroids are spread very far apart. Ceres, a dwarf planet, lives here.

objects.label: Jupiter
objects.info: The largest planet - over 11 times Earth's width. A gas giant with the Great Red Spot storm and dozens of moons including Io and Europa.

objects.label: Saturn
objects.info: A gas giant famous for bright rings of ice and rock. It is so light for its size that its average density is less than water's.

objects.label: Saturn's rings

objects.label: Uranus
objects.info: An ice giant tipped on its side (axis tilted about 98 degrees). Methane in its air gives a blue-green colour.

objects.label: Neptune
objects.info: The farthest planet, about 30 times Earth's distance from the Sun. It has supersonic winds and takes about 165 years to orbit once.

objects.label: Singularity (idealised)
objects.info: In classical general relativity the mass is squeezed to a point of infinite density. Physicists think new physics (quantum gravity) is needed there.

objects.label: Event horizon
objects.info: The boundary beyond which nothing - not even light - can escape. Its radius for a non-spinning black hole is r = 2GM/c2.

objects.label: Photon sphere
objects.info: At 1.5 times the horizon radius, light can orbit the black hole in unstable circular paths.

objects.label: Accretion disk
objects.info: Hot, glowing gas spiralling in. Friction heats it to millions of degrees so it shines brightly in X-rays.

objects.label: Jet (north)
objects.info: Some black holes launch narrow beams of particles at nearly light speed along the spin axis, powered by magnetic fields.

objects.label: Jet (south)
objects.info: The jet usually appears on both sides of the disk.

objects.label: Companion star
objects.info: In an X-ray binary, a normal star donates gas to the black hole - which is how many stellar-mass black holes are found.

objects.label: Bent light ray
objects.info: Light passing near a massive object follows curved space. Near a black hole this bending (gravitational lensing) is extreme.

steps.title: Tips

steps.title: Please read first

steps.title: Types
steps.body: Physical harm. Emotional harm like insults or threats. Financial abuse such as taking money or property without consent. Neglect, which means not giving food, care or medicines. Abandonment. Sexual abuse.

steps.title: Warning signs
steps.body: Unexplained injuries, fear of a person, sudden changes in money or property, weight loss, poor hygiene, being kept away from others.

steps.title: Danger now
steps.body: If someone is in danger now, call 112. For guidance or reports, call Elderline 14567.

steps.title: Anyone can be involved

lessons.title: What the Act says, in general terms

scenes.text: Mrs Lal learned about a law for parents.

steps.title: The Act
steps.body: The Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 says children, and in some cases relatives who inherit property, have a duty to maintain parents and senior citizens who cannot maintain themselves.

steps.title: How it works in general
steps.body: A senior can apply to a Maintenance Tribunal for monthly maintenance. The Act also speaks of old-age homes and protection of life and property of seniors. The process aims to be quick and simple. Rules are made by states.

steps.title: Property transfers
steps.body: If a senior transferred property on the condition of being looked after and the condition is not met, the transfer may be treated as void in some cases. Ask a lawyer.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. Talk to a lawyer, legal-aid office or Elderline 14567.

life-senior-health.description: General health education for seniors and families: blood pressure, diabetes, falls, exercise and yoga, eyes, ears and teeth, memory, medicines, food and sleep. Not medical advice; see a doctor and call 112 in an emergency.

courses.title: Blood pressure and diabetes, day by day
courses.summary: Understand blood pressure and blood sugar readings, healthy habits, and the signs that need a doctor or an emergency call.

scenes.text: Mr Shetty measured his BP at home: 150 over 95.
He wrote it in a notebook and took it to the doctor.

steps.title: Please read first
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Two numbers
steps.body: The top number is **systolic**. The bottom is **diastolic**. Around 120/80 is often called normal. Readings of 140/90 or more on repeated checks are commonly treated as high. Your doctor sets your own target.

steps.title: Measure well
steps.body: Sit quietly for 5 minutes. Feet flat. Arm at heart level. Same time each day. Write it down.

steps.title: Habits
steps.body: Less salt (WHO suggests under 5 grams a day), regular walks, no tobacco, limited alcohol, and taking medicines as advised.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: Do not stop BP tablets on your own. See a doctor for repeated high readings, dizziness, or fainting. Call 112 for sudden severe headache, chest pain, weakness on one side or trouble speaking.

scenes.text: Mrs Dsouza felt shaky and sweaty before lunch.

steps.title: High and low
steps.body: **High sugar** can cause thirst, passing urine often and tiredness. **Low sugar** (hypoglycaemia) can cause shakiness, sweating, hunger, confusion.

steps.title: If low and awake
steps.body: People on diabetes medicines are often told to take quick sugar (like juice or glucose) and recheck. Follow your doctor's plan.

steps.title: If confused or unconscious
steps.body: Do not put food in the mouth of someone who cannot swallow. Call 112.

steps.title: Daily care
steps.body: Check feet daily for cuts. Eat regular meals. Take medicines as advised. Keep HbA1c checks as your doctor advises.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: See a doctor for repeated high or low readings, a foot wound that does not heal, or sudden vision change.

steps.title: Heart attack signs
steps.body: Chest pressure or pain, pain in the arm, jaw or back, breathlessness, cold sweat. Some people, including many older women and people with diabetes, have mild or unusual signs.

steps.title: Act, do not wait
steps.body: Call 112 immediately. Do not drive yourself. Note the time symptoms began.

steps.title: Please read first
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Common causes
steps.body: Slippery floors, loose rugs, poor light, loose slippers, dizziness from medicines or low BP, poor eyesight, and weak legs.

steps.title: Fix the home
steps.body: Good light on the path to the toilet at night. Remove loose rugs. Grab bars in the bathroom. Sturdy chappals or shoes.

steps.title: Stand up slowly
steps.body: Sit at the bed edge for a minute before standing.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: See a doctor after any fall with head injury, severe pain, or if you cannot bear weight. Call 112 for a serious injury. Tell your doctor if you fall more than once.

steps.title: General guidance
steps.body: WHO advises adults, including older adults, about **150 minutes** of moderate activity each week, plus muscle-strengthening on 2 days and balance work for older adults. Start slowly if you are new.

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Walking or cycling for the heart. Light strength work for muscles. Balance practice for fall protection. Stretching for comfort.

steps.title: Talk test
steps.body: You should be able to talk while walking. If you cannot speak, slow down.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: Check with your doctor before starting if you have heart disease, uncontrolled BP, chest pain, dizziness, or joint problems. Stop and call 112 for chest pain or severe breathlessness.

steps.title: Joints

steps.title: Please read first
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Common conditions
steps.body: **Cataract:** clouding of the lens. **Glaucoma:** raised eye pressure that harms the nerve, often without early pain. **Diabetic eye disease** and age-related macular problems also occur.

steps.title: Checks
steps.body: Have a full eye check each year or as your doctor advises, especially with diabetes.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Good lighting at home. Use glasses that match your current prescription.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: Sudden loss of vision, flashes of light, a curtain over the vision, or a painful red eye need urgent care. Call 112 or go to an emergency room.

steps.title: Signs

steps.title: Do
steps.body: Get a hearing test. Hearing aids can help many people. Wax can also block the ear; do not poke it with sticks.

steps.title: Talking to someone with hearing loss
steps.body: Face them. Speak clearly, not shouting. Reduce background noise.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: See a doctor for sudden hearing loss in one ear, ear pain with discharge, or dizziness with hearing change.

steps.title: Dry mouth

steps.title: Please read first
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Often normal
steps.body: Forgetting a name and remembering later. Misplacing things sometimes. Missing a word occasionally.

steps.title: Possible warning signs
steps.body: Forgetting recent events often. Repeating the same questions. Getting lost in familiar places. Trouble with money or cooking you used to do easily. Big changes in mood or behaviour. Trouble following a conversation.

steps.title: Do not panic
steps.body: Memory problems can come from many causes. Some are treatable, such as low vitamin B12, thyroid problems, depression, infection, sleep problems, or medicine side effects.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: See a doctor if the changes are new, getting worse, or affect daily life. Bring a family member who can describe what they see.

steps.title: Support

steps.title: Look-alike strips

steps.title: When to see a doctor

steps.title: Interactions
steps.body: Some medicines change how others work. Some cold, pain and herbal products can raise BP or cause dizziness. Alcohol can interact with many medicines.

steps.title: Ask the pharmacist

steps.title: Pain medicines
steps.body: Overuse of some pain tablets can harm kidneys, stomach or liver. Paracetamol overdose can damage the liver. Follow the label or your doctor.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: Call your doctor for new dizziness, rash, black stools, confusion or swelling after starting a medicine. Call 112 for breathing trouble or swelling of the face.

steps.title: Please read first
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Plate idea
steps.body: Half the plate: vegetables and fruit. A quarter: whole grains such as roti, millets or brown rice. A quarter: protein such as dal, pulses, eggs, fish, paneer or curd.

steps.title: Protein
steps.body: Older people often need enough protein to keep muscles strong. Spread it across meals. Ask your doctor if you have a kidney condition.

steps.title: Less salt and sugar
steps.body: WHO suggests under 5 g of salt a day. Limit sweets and fried snacks.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: See a doctor for unplanned weight loss, loss of appetite for weeks, or trouble swallowing. Diet needs differ with diabetes, kidney or heart conditions; ask your doctor or a dietitian.

steps.title: Why
steps.body: With age, the sense of thirst can reduce. Not drinking enough can cause tiredness, constipation, urinary infections and dizziness.

steps.title: Habit
steps.body: Sip through the day. Include soups, buttermilk, coconut water or fruit. Follow your doctor's advice if you have heart or kidney conditions that limit fluids.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: See a doctor for very dark urine, extreme thirst, confusion or fainting, especially in hot weather.

steps.title: Sleep after 60
steps.body: Many older adults sleep less deeply. About 7 to 8 hours is a common aim, but needs differ.

steps.title: Habits
steps.body: Same wake-up time daily. Morning light and a walk. Limit tea and coffee after noon. Avoid heavy dinners and screens late at night. Keep the bedroom dark and cool.

steps.title: Sleeping tablets
steps.body: Do not use sleeping tablets or alcohol for sleep without asking a doctor. They can raise the risk of falls and confusion.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: See a doctor for loud snoring with pauses in breathing, daytime sleepiness, or sleeplessness lasting weeks, or low mood.
